subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the AQA spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE AQA Chemistry simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Tests for carbonates, sulfates and halides

questions.q: In chemistry, a pure substance is:
options: A single element or single compound not mixed with anything else
Any substance that is safe to drink
A mixture with only two components
questions.explain: In chemistry, pure means a single element or single compound, not the everyday meaning of clean or natural.

questions.q: How can you use melting and boiling points to check if a substance is pure?
options: A pure substance melts and boils at a specific, sharp temperature
A pure substance melts over a wide range of temperatures
Pure substances have no fixed melting point
Impurities always raise the melting point
questions.explain: Pure substances have sharp, fixed melting and boiling points. Impurities lower and broaden the melting point over a range.

questions.q: A formulation is:
options: A random mixture with unknown amounts
A useful mixture with each component in a carefully measured quantity for a purpose
An element that has been purified
questions.explain: A formulation is a mixture designed as a useful product, with each component present in a carefully controlled amount.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a formulation?
options: Paint, made of pigment, binder, solvent and additives in set proportions
A single crystal of sodium chloride
questions.explain: Paint is a formulation because it is a mixture with each ingredient in a precise proportion designed for a purpose.

questions.q: In paper chromatography, the two phases are:
options: A stationary phase (the paper) and a mobile phase (the solvent)
questions.explain: Chromatography relies on a stationary phase (the chromatography paper) and a mobile phase (the moving solvent).

questions.q: A spot travels 4 cm while the solvent front travels 8 cm. What is the Rf value?
questions.explain: Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent = 4 / 8 = 0.5.

questions.q: How many spots would a single pure substance show on a chromatogram?
questions.explain: A pure substance produces a single spot in all solvents, whereas a mixture separates into several spots.

questions.q: The test for hydrogen gas is:
options: A lit splint gives a squeaky pop
questions.explain: Hydrogen makes a squeaky pop when a lit splint is held near it, as the hydrogen burns rapidly.

questions.q: The test for oxygen gas is:
options: The gas turns damp litmus red
A lit splint gives a squeaky pop
questions.explain: Oxygen relights a glowing splint because it supports combustion.

questions.q: The test for carbon dioxide is:
options: Damp litmus paper is bleached white
Bubble the gas through limewater, which turns cloudy
A lit splint gives a squeaky pop
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide turns limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) milky or cloudy.

questions.q: The test for chlorine gas is:
options: A lit splint gives a squeaky pop
Damp blue litmus paper is bleached white (turning red first)
questions.explain: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper white (it may briefly turn red as chlorine is acidic before bleaching).

questions.q: Which metal ion gives a lilac (purple) flame test colour?
questions.explain: Potassium gives a lilac flame. Sodium is yellow, calcium orange-red, copper green, and lithium crimson.

questions.q: A metal salt produces a crimson (red) flame. Which ion is present?
questions.explain: Lithium ions produce a crimson red flame in a flame test.

questions.q: Adding sodium hydroxide solution to a solution produces a blue precipitate. Which metal ion is present?
questions.explain: Copper(II) ions give a blue precipitate with NaOH. Iron(II) gives green, iron(III) gives brown, calcium gives white.

questions.q: A brown precipitate forms when NaOH is added to a solution. Which ion is present?
questions.explain: Iron(III) ions give a brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide with sodium hydroxide solution.

questions.lo: Tests for carbonates, sulfates and halides
questions.q: To test for carbonate ions, you add dilute acid and look for:
options: Fizzing that produces a gas turning limewater cloudy
questions.explain: Carbonates react with dilute acid to release carbon dioxide (fizzing), which turns limewater cloudy.

questions.lo: Tests for carbonates, sulfates and halides
questions.q: The test for sulfate ions uses barium chloride solution (with dilute HCl) and gives:
options: A white precipitate of barium sulfate
questions.explain: Sulfate ions give a white precipitate of barium sulfate when barium chloride (acidified with HCl) is added.

questions.lo: Tests for carbonates, sulfates and halides
questions.q: Adding silver nitrate (with dilute nitric acid) to a halide solution gives a cream precipitate. The halide is:
questions.explain: With silver nitrate: chloride gives white, bromide gives cream, and iodide gives yellow precipitate.

questions.q: One advantage of instrumental methods over chemical tests is that they:
options: Are more accurate, more sensitive and faster on small samples
questions.explain: Instrumental methods are rapid, highly accurate and sensitive, and can analyse very small samples, unlike simpler chemical tests.

questions.q: Which instrumental method is used to identify metal ions using the light they emit?
questions.explain: Flame emission spectroscopy analyses the light emitted by metal ions in a flame to identify and measure their concentration.
